title: Write a new classifier
question: Can the same photograph answer a question the old classifier head never had a label for?
try: Replace these with Newfoundland, pug, and Persian. Then try indoors and outdoors.
lesson: The description supplies a comparison vector. Changing the candidates does not train or replace the image encoder.

title: Ask about a property
question: Can a description be more specific than an object category?
try: Compare ‘a white cup’, ‘a red cup’, and ‘a blue cup’. Keep the photograph fixed.
lesson: Natural language lets us propose attributes, materials and contexts. These are hypotheses to test, not guaranteed abilities.

title: Find a photo with words
question: Could you find a photo without knowing its filename?
try: Search for ‘a pet’, ‘a spacecraft taking off’, then ‘a laptop’. Is the best available result always relevant?
lesson: Encode the gallery once. A new query needs only a text embedding and dot products. Search always has a nearest item even when nothing matches.

title: Choose a description
candidates: a rocket launching into the night sky
a tall building beside a river
question: Is selecting a sentence the same as writing one?
try: Write your own competing descriptions. Include one that mentions only part of the scene.
lesson: CLIP ranks supplied text. It does not generate captions. A caption generator requires additional machinery.

title: Find visually related images
question: Can we search without any words at all?
try: Choose a cat, dog or portrait as the query. Predict the nearest other image before running.
lesson: The image encoder is useful on its own. Similarity can suggest groups or possible duplicates; it cannot certify that two files are duplicates.

title: What changed?
question: Does ‘with hat’ minus ‘without hat’ point towards the word ‘hat’?
try: Swap the images. Then try blue mug minus red mug with the words blue, red, cup, and hat.
lesson: Inspired by CodeEmporium’s hat experiment, using our own generated pair. This is an exploratory direction, not a trained change detector. Subtle image differences remain. Cosine is not a probability of the change.

title: Remove the right answer
question: What happens when every offered label is wrong?
try: Run once, then add ‘a photo of a dog’. Compare each cosine with its share of the softmax.
lesson: Softmax distributes 100% across the choices you provide. It is not calibrated confidence that the best label is true.

title: Try to break the model
question: Does the word ‘without’ reliably reverse what a phrase means?
try: Try negation, counting, and two descriptions with reversed relations. Save a failure as well as a success.
lesson: A flexible vocabulary does not guarantee precise compositional reasoning. Report what this checkpoint does on these examples, not universal claims.

title: Search an overhead landscape
candidates: an aerial image of a brick kiln
an aerial image of a solar farm
an aerial image of agricultural fields
an aerial image of industrial warehouses
question: What would a sustainability researcher want to retrieve?
lesson: The search idea transfers to satellite tiles, but synthetic images are not evidence of field performance. Real deployment needs georeferenced imagery, independent labels, and evaluation across regions and resolutions.
try: Compare all four overhead scenes. Try ‘brick kiln’ alone, then a longer description. These scenes are synthetic.

title: Recognize the kind of medical image
question: Does recognizing an imaging modality mean the model can diagnose a disease?
lesson: This public radiograph supports a modality-matching lesson, not diagnosis. General CLIP scores are not clinical evidence; medical tasks need domain-specific validation.
try: Compare modality descriptions first. Notice how different this image is from an everyday photograph.

title: Keep the concept; change the style
question: Can the model recognize a dog when the texture of a photograph disappears?
lesson: This is a small domain-shift experiment. A success here does not establish robustness to every drawing style.
try: Switch between the generated photo and sketch. Replace ‘a drawing of’ with ‘a photo of’ and compare.

title: A second subtraction experiment
question: Does the embedding difference capture a color change as well as an added object?
lesson: Difference directions depend on images, normalization and wording. They are exploratory measurements, not guaranteed semantic algebra.
try: Reverse the pair. Try ‘a blue mug’ and ‘a red mug’ instead of single words.
sourceLabel: Extension of the CodeEmporium subtraction idea

title: Add a chimney
question: Does adding a chimney produce a useful direction?
lesson: Synthetic paired scenes test a hypothesis. Shadows and fine details also change; this is not a causal proof or a validated kiln detector.
sourceLabel: Our extension of CodeEmporium’s subtraction experiment
try: Predict the winner, run, then reverse the pair. Edit the candidate words and save the results.

title: Add a visible medical device
question: Does the difference emphasize the added device?
lesson: Both radiographs are generated illustrations. Anatomy and device placement are approximate. This measures concept matching on synthetic pictures, not diagnostic or clinical performance.
sourceLabel: Our extension of CodeEmporium’s subtraction experiment
try: Predict the winner, run, then reverse the pair. Edit the candidate words and save the results.

title: Change style, keep the dog
question: Does subtracting the photo from the sketch emphasize style?
lesson: This subtraction includes background and rendering changes. Compare original image-to-text matching with the difference direction; a successful guess does not isolate a causal concept.
sourceLabel: Our extension of CodeEmporium’s subtraction experiment
try: Predict the winner, run, then reverse the pair. Edit the candidate words and save the results.
